result.question: How do latency and bandwidth differ, and which direction of change is preferable for each?
result.answer:
- **Latency** is the time you have to wait before an operation starts producing its result/data (or the time between the start and completion of an event). Lower latency is preferable because it means a better/faster response.
- **Bandwidth** (or throughput) is the total amount of work done or data transferred in a given time (per unit of time). Higher bandwidth is preferable because it means more data can be transferred per second.

retrieved_chunks.text: LATENCY AND BANDWIDTH • Latency = the time you have to wait before an operation starts producing its result/data. • Latency tells us "How long do I have to wait?“ • Suppose the CPU requests data from RAM and the first byte of data arrives after 100 ns. • Lower latency = better/faster response.

PERFORMANCE TRENDS: BANDWIDTH OVER LATENCY • Bandwidth or throughput is the total amount of work done in a given time, such as megabytes per second for a disk transfer. • In contrast, latency or response time is the time between the start and the completion of an event, such as milliseconds for a disk access. • A simple rule of thumb is that bandwidth grows by at least the square of the improvement in latency. Computer designers should plan accordingly.

LATENCY AND BANDWIDTH • Bandwidth = the amount of data that can be transferred per unit of time. • Bandwidth tells us "How much data can I transfer per second?“ • It is usually measured in: MB/s GB/s • Higher bandwidth = more data can be transferred per second.

ENERGY EFFICIENCY STRATEGIES • Overclocking. • Intel started offering T urbomode in 2008, where the chip decides that it is safe to run at a higher clock rate for a short time, possibly on just a few cores, until temperature starts to rise. For example, the 3.3 GHz Core i7 can run in short bursts for 3.6 GHz. Indeed, the highest-performing microprocessors each year since 2008 have all offered temporary overclocking of about 10% over the nominal clock rate. • For single-threaded code, these microprocessors can turn off all cores but one and run it faster. Note that, although the operating system can turn off T urbomode, there is no notification once it is enabled, so the programmers may be surprised to see their programs vary in performance because of room temperature.
